video_title: AI Can Build Your Portfolio—But Can You Trust It? | Systematic Investor | Ep.419
gist: Alan Dunn and Nick review a strong 2026 for trend following (SG Trend and SG CTA about +15% YTD, driven by short bonds as the 10-year breaks above 5%), discuss a GS chart showing 45% of S&P 500 stocks with negative beta, an Alpha Architect study finding no edge from VIX-conditioned momentum lookbacks, and Andrew Ang's agentic-AI asset allocation paper.

themes.theme: Trend following performance and the bond-short trade

insights.claim: SG Trend and the SG CTA Index were each up about 3.7% in September through the 23rd and about 15.2% year-to-date, with roughly 80% of the month's gain across the managers Nick allocates to coming from short fixed-income positions, including the long end.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: Trend following is having a very strong year and September P&L is concentrated in one macro trade, short bonds.

insights.claim: Nick cites stats ranking 2026 as the third-best year for trend following in the last 15, behind 2014 and 2022, and says rates only began trending around Q2 after earlier lack of trendiness, with rates doubling their contribution to performance in September versus commodities and equities.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Rate trends are a recent driver, so the year's performance leans on a regime that has only just established itself.

insights.claim: An investor who moves part of a 60/40 allocation into trend following ends up net short bonds in a yield spike, so the trend sleeve offsets the loss on the core long-bond position.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: This is the textbook case for trend as a diversifier when bonds stop hedging.

insights.claim: Even after a sizable move in yields, bond-market volatility has stayed contained, and since trend signals are volatility-scaled their strength has not grown, meaning the yield move has been larger than the volatility it came with.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: A smooth, low-vol grind keeps trend positions held and the P&L attribution greater than in a choppy run-up.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield had been in a range of about 3.5% to 5% since October 2022, with the market pricing a recession roughly three times, and has now moved above 5% as growth expectations flipped positive.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: A multi-year range break is what trend strategies feed on.

insights.claim: In September, equities were slightly negative (less than a percentage point) after trend followers entered long, commodities were flat apart from energy, softs added nothing, and currencies were trendless given dollar moves, so rates were effectively the only story.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Single-factor concentration in rates means a bond reversal would hit trend returns hard.

themes.theme: Why yields are rising and what it means

insights.claim: Alan notes the 2-year yield has risen at least 75 basis points since mid-August with short ends repricing globally, as if the market has become bullish on global growth or expects the conflict in Iran to last longer.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: The repricing is led by the front end, implying the driver is policy and growth expectations rather than purely fiscal worries.

insights.claim: Analysts wrongly look for a linear, proportionate cause-and-effect between fundamentals and market moves; markets are complex adaptive systems where positioning, barriers and hedges mean the same fundamental change can have a big or small impact.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: Single-cause stories for the yield rise (deficits, AI spending, debasement) are probably overfitted.

insights.claim: As recently as January and February analysts projected rate cuts and a normalization phase, so the current move to multi-year yield records in the US and UK is a sharp reversal of consensus within about six months.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Consensus rate forecasts have been unreliable over a six-month horizon.

insights.claim: Alan lists the competing explanations for the yield rise as economic growth, fiscal concerns, higher expected average rates, competition for capital from budget deficits or AI spend, and debasement or credibility issues.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunn (host)
insights.so_what: The attribution debate is unresolved, so positioning risk exists on any single narrative.

insights.claim: A Goldman Sachs chart from Christian Mulman shows about 45% of S&P 500 constituents have a negative beta to the index on a 3-month calculation, versus just under 20% at the dot-com peak, when the last comparable situation occurred.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Extreme index concentration means half the market is decoupled from the index, raising stock selection and dispersion significance.

insights.claim: The negative-beta surge is attributed to AI dominance building its own mini index within the cap-weighted S&P 500 while the rest of the stocks become less correlated to it.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Index-level moves mask very different behavior beneath the surface.

insights.claim: The decoupling creates opportunities for dispersion trades, and some market participants talk about going long correlation, alongside a debate on whether bonds remain defensive in the current environment.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Dispersion and correlation positioning are the live trades around AI concentration.

insights.claim: An Alpha Architect note extended a 2017 study of VIX-dependent momentum lookbacks (shorter windows when VIX is high, longer when low) and found no significant value beyond a static 10-month lookback after nine more years of data.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Adjusting lookback by volatility regime does not reliably improve simple momentum.

insights.claim: The study's design is a long-only monthly-rebalanced pick of the best one or two of five ETFs with equal notional weights and no volatility scaling, so it resembles retail cross-sectional momentum rather than directional trend following.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Its findings do not transfer directly to institutional CTA-style trend models.

insights.claim: The apparent outperformance of the VIX-conditioned variant is concentrated in a few months, notably November 2020 after the Covid vaccine announcement, and the high-VIX regime had only three observations, so statistical power is very low.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Trigger-based strategies rest on a handful of activations and cannot be statistically validated.

insights.claim: Nick prefers scaling signals continuously by volatility and correlation within portfolio design and risk budgeting over discrete VIX triggers, because triggers by nature activate rarely and parameterize heavily.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Continuous volatility use avoids regime-classification overfitting.

insights.claim: Nick argues that if trends do not exist, a trend model should not be made more complex to recreate them, and that investors should instead add complementary systematic strategies that benefit from those regimes.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Diversifying the sleeve beats parameter-heavy attempts to time trend regimes.

insights.claim: A faster trend model would improve turning-point response, but the open question is whether speed can be deployed dynamically in time; Nick asks any indicator claiming to time turning points to reveal its false positives, since picking 3 of 33 right proves little.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Judge timing signals by false-positive rate, not by hits.

insights.claim: Sharp V-shaped market reversals occur about once per year over the last four years, including the Liberation Day episode, and have scarred trend followers, while the March 2026 event was less contagious.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Short-lived spikes that reverse quickly are a recurring risk for unconstrained trend followers.

themes.theme: Agentic AI for asset allocation (Andrew Ang paper)

insights.claim: Andrew Ang, formerly head of factor investing at BlackRock, with new firm Oldbridge, published a paper on an agentic architecture where macro, asset-class, covariance, 19 portfolio-construction, researcher and adversarial-diversifier agents feed a CIO agent that writes a board memo.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: This blueprint shows how institutional asset allocation workflows may be automated under human supervision.

insights.claim: In the paper's March 2026 test, the macro agent classified the regime as late-cycle with stagflationary risk, and the CIO agent chose an allocation of about 44% equities against a 60/40 benchmark, favoring heuristic and risk-based schemes over those using capital market assumptions.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Under an unclear macro regime the agentic process leaned towards diversification and away from return forecasts.

insights.claim: Nick's reading is that when the macro regime is mixed or unobservable, portfolios should diversify and rely on risk-oriented or heuristic allocation rather than trust capital market assumptions.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Allocation conviction should scale with regime clarity.

insights.claim: Backtesting LLM-based allocation is problematic because models embed knowledge of the future, agents may vote for better-performing schemes in hindsight, and LLM outputs are non-deterministic so identical prompts can give different results, which blocks reproducibility.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Agentic products cannot be validated with standard historical backtests.

insights.claim: The paper flags monoculture risk: if all agents use the same LLM from one provider, their outputs become correlated.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Widespread use of the same foundation model could create correlated allocation errors.

insights.claim: The paper's opening argues the most binding constraint in asset management is the finite bandwidth of human decision makers rather than data or model sophistication, a point Nick links to why clients value trend following's ability to deploy faster than an investment board can act.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Speed of decision-to-deployment is itself a source of edge for systematic strategies.

insights.claim: Nick expects agentic AI to make multi-objective portfolio design (such as crisis alpha, drawdown limits and absolute return) more accessible but still requiring human expertise, and says the bar for AI-run index products is higher so timing of labeled AI-agent products is hard to foresee.
insights.speaker: Nick Palus (guest, systematic investor)
insights.so_what: Near-term adoption is more likely as supervised tooling than as autonomous labeled products.
